Sacco and Vanzetti. In May 1920, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, Italian immigrant anarchists, were arrested for a payroll robbery and murder in South Braintree, Massachusetts. Convicted largely on contested ballistic evidence and tried in an atmosphere of anti-radical hysteria, they were executed in 1927. The case became a symbol of injustice, judicial bias, and the persecution of political dissidents in post-war America.

A payroll robbery and murder occurred on April 15, 1920, in South Braintree, Massachusetts. Fifteen thousand seven hundred and seventy-six dollars were stolen, and two men were killed, including security guard Frederick Parmenter. Sacco was a shoemaker, and Vanzetti was a fish peddler, both known anarchist sympathizers. They were arrested in May 1920, with police suspecting them based on their political affiliations and an altercation with police in a prior raid.

The prosecution's case rested heavily on ballistic evidence. A bullet recovered from the victims allegedly matched a test-fired bullet from Sacco's pistol, analyzed by expert Charles Van Amburgh, though that matching was later disputed. The trial judge, Webster Thayer, was openly hostile to the defendants and made disparaging remarks about anarchistic bastards that were later documented. The jury was composed of men with anti-anarchist bias.

Despite weaknesses in identification evidence and ballistic analysis, Sacco and Vanzetti were convicted in July 1921. An appeal process dragged on for six years amid international outrage and demonstrations. Both men were executed by electric chair on August 23, 1927. Vanzetti's last words, I am innocent, reinforced belief in their innocence among supporters and later investigators.

Modern ballistic analysis and archival re-examination, including the identification of evidence via newer techniques in 1961, have deepened suspicion that Sacco and Vanzetti were innocent or that the evidence was fabricated, marking the case as foundational to critiques of American criminal procedure and bias.
